description: Stellar Syntax is a team of six engineers from Lusaka, Zambia, turning code into solutions for space and Earth. We build with creativity, precision, and a love for solving real-world problems, one line of code at a time.
summary:
Artemis is a software-based astronaut health-monitoring system developed by Team CosmoCeck. It addresses the challenge of helping astronauts continuously evaluate and respond to changes in their health during space missions. Artemis combines personalized dashboards with an AI assistant called ASTRA, which uses MediaPipe-powered motion intelligence to guide astronauts through simple movements and assess indicators such as posture, coordination, and physical condition. ASTRA also conducts quick daily check-ins, allowing astronauts to log symptoms and wellbeing indicators—including stress, headaches, or fever—through simple yes-or-no responses.

Artemis is important because it makes health monitoring convenient, fast, and user-friendly while supporting consistent physical routines. By identifying concerns earlier and helping astronauts maintain their conditioning, the system may improve mission readiness and support a smoother recovery after returning to Earth. Future versions will integrate additional probes and wearable devices for richer health data.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Artemis is a web-based health monitoring system that helps astronauts check their own health and act on it when Earth is too far away to answer in real time. Its AI assistant, ASTRA, talks directly to the astronaut and guides them through simple movements. Using MediaPipe pose tracking and the webcam, it measures joint angles, posture, symmetry and repetitions and scores the result. ASTRA also asks yes/no questions about stress, headache, fever and other symptoms, and logs the answers each day. Artemis tracks sleep duration, quality and bedtime, assesses stress level and gives a recommendation. A 2D simulated body anatomy shows the astronaut’s movements.

Under the hood, Artemis keeps three stages separate:

  • Observation: movement metrics, sleep logs, check-ins and symptoms are recorded.
  • Inference: a rule engine built from a 316-record dataset of healthy and unhealthy astronaut signs checks those records against reference targets and trends.
  • Recommendation: countermeasures and next steps are drawn from the dataset and spaceflight research.

Each alert shows which records caused it. The decision logic runs on the device, so it keeps working through communication delays of up to about 20 minutes one way. Personalized dashboards, a health timeline and a PostgreSQL backend with accounts support the rest.

What benefits does it have?

  • Health checks are convenient, fast and easy to use, through voice and yes/no answers.
  • Astronauts keep a physical routine in flight, which reduces recovery time back on Earth.
  • Several data sources replace reliance on one wristband.
  • Alerts are explainable, so astronauts and flight surgeons can see why one fired.
  • It works offline during communication delays.

What is the intended impact?
Artemis gives astronauts on deep-space missions a way to spot health changes early and respond without waiting for Earth. It addresses the limits of the current ARCHeR wristband: a wristband is not a complete system, stress is hard to infer from physiology alone, and wearable data quality may degrade in space. We plan to add hardware such as probes and wearable devices. The same approach could also help with remote health monitoring on Earth.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did we use?

  • Languages and frameworks: TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS and PHP.
  • Computer vision and AI: MediaPipe Pose Landmarker. Gemini Live and browser speech are used for voice, with browser speech as the fallback.
  • Data: PostgreSQL through PHP PDO, plus browser storage (IndexedDB and localStorage). PHP scripts validated the dataset.
  • Development tools: Git and GitHub. Claude, Gemini and ChatGPT were used as development and research assistants. They are not part of the running application.
  • Hardware: an ordinary device with a webcam and microphone. Probes and wearables are future work.

How is it creative?

  • ASTRA turns a webcam into a health sensor and acts as a conversational movement coach.
  • Observation, inference and recommendation are kept separate.
  • Alerts come from deterministic rules built from a dataset, not a black-box model, and the records behind each alert are highlighted on the timeline.
  • The anatomy view shows movement visually.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Communication delay: the up-to-20-minute delay led to offline, on-device decision support.
  • Safety: Artemis is a prototype, and its outputs are not diagnoses or medical advice.
  • Dataset honesty: the dataset is a reference compilation, not real astronaut records, and has not been clinically validated. NASA’s individual astronaut records are not publicly available.
  • Privacy and security: authentication, sessions and CSRF protection are in place. Role-based access, audit logging and HTTPS are still needed.
  • Usability: colour-coded severity badges and simple yes/no interaction suit a high-workload environment.
  • Research quality: we verified claims against NASA and CSA pages and labelled anything we could not confirm.
  • Remaining work: registration, the database import and full integration testing are not yet complete.
